The majority of work on the AoA effect has been in monomorphemic words and findings may not directly translate to compound words, which represent the majority of Englishlanguage words (Mousikou et al., 2019). The majority of words in the world are complex; compound words are a key example of complex words, and are commonplace in various languages such as English, Chinese and Finnish (Bertram & Hyona, 2003; Elsherif et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2024). In English, compound words (e.g. "airport") are formed from two lexemes: the modifier (e.g. "air" in "airport") and the head (i.e. "port" in "airport"). The modifier narrows the semantic domain of the head (e.g. air specifies that an airport is a port for aeroplanes rather than boats; Benczes, 2005 Benczes, , 2014 Benczes, , 2015;; Günther et al., 2020). The head sets the broader semantic category, establishes the morphosyntactic features of the compound word as a whole, and establishes the word class 1 . Compound words are, by definition, polysyllabic. Thus, as compared to monosyllabic words, compound words have a more complex orthography and phonology and require more processing time (Cortese & Schock, 2013). This extended processing time allows the word's semantic properties to play a more significant role in the overall recognition of compound words (Elsherif et al., 2019).

Thus, the processing of compound words is qualitatively different to that of monomorphemic words. It is therefore not appropriate to generalise findings from monomorphemic words to morphologically complex words such as compound words.

The spacing within English compound words may also influence processing. English compound words show variation in their orthographic form or spatial layout, and are typically categorised as open/spaced (e.g., "ice cream"), hyphenated (e.g., "long-term"), and closed/unspaced (e.g., "blackboard"). This classification is not always rigid, as different dictionaries may disagree on the proper spacing of certain compounds (Juhasz et al., 2005; Kuperman & Bertram, 2013). Broader evidence indicates that even minimal changes in the presentation of the compound word's spatial layout can fundamentally shift how the compound word is processed, specifically in terms of its morphemic salience (how easily the component parts are recognised) and the semantic relationship between its constituents (Bertram, 2011; Elsherif et al., 2019; Elsherif & Catling, 2023 , 2024; Frisson et al., 2007; Inhoff et al., 2000). A spaced presentation consistently encourages morphological decomposition, necessitating an additional processing step: the need to merge the two lexemes to access the meaning of the compound word. This requirement arises because the spaced format introduces competition between the individual constituent meanings and the meaning of the compound as a whole (Brooks & de Garcia, 2015; Kuperman, 2013).

Despite theoretical models suggesting that the orthographic form of compound words influence their processing, empirical evidence regarding the impact of spacing remains nuanced. Several studies indicate that spaced compounds generally incur a processing cost relative to unspaced counterparts. For instance, Juhasz and Berkowitz (2011) reported longer reading times in eye-tracking for spaced compounds and Elsherif and Catling (2023) observed that spaced words resulted in slower decision times during memory tasks.

Furthermore, research has consistently shown that the AoA of the constituent morphemes influence processing speed when compounds are presented in their spaced form, suggesting that spacing may modulate how lexical components are integrated (Elsherif & Catling, 2021 , 2024; Elsherif et al., 2019). However, some empirical evidence contradicts the general trend; for instance, Inhoff et al. (2000) observed that introducing spaces into German compounds actually facilitated processing speed, and Elsherif and Catling (2024) found that spaced compounds were recognized more quickly than unspaced compounds in lexical decision tasks. These conflicting findings highlight a significant lack of consensus in the literature, suggesting that the processing costs of spaced versus unspaced compounds may be highly task-dependent.

The likelihood of observing an AoA effect, whether for the compound as a whole or for its individual constituents, is fundamentally linked to orthographic spacing. Evidence consistently demonstrates that the AoA of the whole compound reliably influences processing across both spaced and unspaced presentations (Elsherif et al., 2019). However, the role of morphemic AoA is more variable: it appears to drive processing speed primarily when compounds are presented in their spaced form. Specifically, research has shown that the AoA of the modifier and head constituents contribute to naming latencies and memory task performance only when the word is spaced (Elsherif et al., 2019; Elsherif & Catling, 2023 , 2024). This suggests that the presence of a space may shift the cognitive load, forcing the system to rely more heavily on constituent-level semantic representations during lexical processing. Given the inconsistent evidence for these effects in eye-tracking, the role of constituent AoA in whole-word processing remains a critical, and unresolved, variable, particularly under varying orthographic conditions.

To date, only one eye-tracking study has examined AoA effects in unspaced compound words during reading. Juhasz (2018) investigated the influence of AoA in 48 young adults.

The authors observed significant AoA effects in GD and TFD but not in FFD and SFD. Juhasz observed that early-acquired compound words were processed more rapidly than later-acquired words, as evidenced by shorter gaze duration and total reading times.

However, there was no effect of individual constituents on reading times. The authors concluded that the representations of the constituents might not be automatically activated during the processing of the whole compound word. Similarly, Kuperman and Bertram (2013) found that reaction times are affected by the properties of the compound word, rather than by the properties of its constituents (but see Elsherif et al., 2019; Elsherif & Catling, 2021 , 2024 , 2026; Juhasz et al., 2003). In sum, while the AoA effect is consistently observed in compound words themselves, the extent to which their constituents contribute to reading behavior remains contentious.

Taken together, the AoA effect is a robust predictor of word recognition across the lifespan and various tasks. According to the integrated account, early-acquired words form stronger, more integrated mappings between orthographic, phonological, and semantic representations. However, the bulk of this evidence stems from monomorphemic words in young adults using response-based tasks. Crucially, three gaps remain that prevent a complete understanding of how developmental learning shapes the mental lexicon. First, while the AoA effect is observed in older adults via behavioral measures, its manifestation in the ecologically valid context of reading, specifically via eye-movement metrics, remains unexplored. Second, although whole-word AoA reliably influences compound processing, the role of constituent-level AoA is contentious, with evidence suggesting that morphemic influences may be masked or constrained by the way a word is visually presented. Third, this potential modulation by orthographic format (spaced vs. unspaced) suggests that spacing alters the fundamental balance between holistic and decomposed processing, a mechanism that has yet to be tested in naturalistic reading. To address these limitations, the present study uses eye-tracking during sentence reading to investigate how the AoA effect is modulated by reader age (young vs. older adults) and compound word format, thereby testing the generalizability of the Integrated Account to more complex populations and lexical items.

By examining AoA effects across both spaced and unspaced compounds, this study provides a unique window into how lexical access evolves across the adult lifespan. While foundational eye-tracking research has established the AoA effect for monomorphemic words (e.g., , Dirix & Duyck, 2017a , 2017b; Guedea et al., 2025; Juhasz et al., 2011; Juhasz & Rayner, 2006; Juhasz & Sheridan, 2020) and compound words (Juhasz, 2018), little is known about how these effects manifest in older adults, whose decades of additional linguistic experience may fundamentally reshape early-learned advantages. Thus, this study investigates how AoA influences reading behaviour across unspaced and spaced compound words and across the adult lifespan (young and older adulthood). Crucially, the orthographic format of compounds, spaced versus unspaced, serves as a functional probe to reveal whether this increased experience facilitates a more holistic approach to lexical access or maintains a reliance on constituent decomposition. By integrating these factors, this research addresses the current gap in ageing literature and provides a rigorous test of whether the Integrated Account's predictions generalize to complex, multi-morphemic structures in naturalistic reading.

The Present Study

We conducted two experiments to evaluate the role of the AoA effect in compound word processing across the lifespan. By manipulating orthographic spacing (spaced vs. unspaced), we sought to determine whether the AoA effect is located at the lexical/semantic level across the lifespan, as posited by Juhasz (2018). We examined whether introducing a space into typically unspaced compound words increased readers' reliance on the earlyacquired semantic representations of the constituent morphemes. Experiment 1 therefore aimed to test AoA effects in unspaced compound words presented within sentences in young and older adults. Experiment 2 investigated these effects when the same words were presented spaced, to assess how spacing influenced the AoA effect in young and older adults. We asked the following research questions: RQ1: Is the AoA effect present in orthographic spacing across the lifespan? RQ2: How do orthographic spacing and age interact to influence the AoA effect during compound word processing?

The following predictions in addressing RQ1 was that in line with previous research (e.g., see review by Elsherif et al., 2023; Inhoff et al., 2000), we first expected a main effect of AoA, where earlier acquired words are more processed more quickly than late-acquired words, and a main effect of spacing, where unspaced words are processed more quickly than spaced words. Building upon this, our predictions for RQ2 expected a smaller AoA effect for spaced compound words than unspaced compound words because the separation may impede direct access to the full compound's lexical-semantic representation (Elsherif, Kirkden et al., 2026). This weakening could also increase competition between the constituents, particularly for later-learned words. We also predicted a two-way interaction between AoA and age. Specifically, we expected the AoA effect to be smaller for older adults than for younger adults. Decades of additional linguistic experience may allow the lexicalsemantic networks of later-learned words to become more entrenched, narrowing the processing gap between early and late acquisitions. Furthermore, the use of eye-tracking allows for the precise measurement of cognitive processes across different stages of reading. Earlier processing measures (e.g., FFD, SFD and GD) primarily reflect initial word identification time and lexical access. Later measures such as TFD capture post-lexical processing, such as semantic integration. The pattern of AoA effects across these measures can therefore be used to further evaluate theoretical accounts. Effects restricted to earlierstage reading (e.g., FFD, GD) would support the Mapping Theory, which attributes AoA advantages to stronger, early-formed mappings created during periods of high neural plasticity. Effects limited to the later stage (TFD/total reading time) would primarily support the Representation Theory, which emphasises that early-learned words are more deeply embedded in semantic networks and thus bias lexical retrieval. Effects observed across both early and late measures would support the integrated account, where early-acquired words benefit simultaneously from richer semantic networks and more efficient orthographic-tophonological mappings.

Method

Power analysis

Recent simulation-based power analyses in reading and eye-tracking (e.g., Schmidtke et al., 2021) emphasize detecting weak main effect slopes (e.g., b = 0.008, as observed in Juhasz, 2018). Consequently, we focused our design and power calculations specifically on detecting critical two-way interactions (e.g., Ageing × AoA, and Spacing × AoA), while adopting a conservative approach to parameter estimation. To reduce experimenter bias, data were analysed after all the participants were recruited and a stopping rule was established prior to data collection. In contrast to compound word studies and AoA using other tasks, eye-tracking evidence concerning the AoA effect remains limited except for Juhasz (2018). We conducted a power analysis, following Elsherif et al. (2019), using Westfall et al.'s (2014) formula for effect size calculation.

Prior to data collection, we conducted a prospective power analysis using Westfall et al.'s (2014) PANGEA framework for linear mixed models. To accommodate our experimental structure, where crossed random factors of participants and items are evaluated alongside the within-subject component for older participants, we parameterised the analysis as a Crossed-by-Condition (CCC) design.

Following Elsherif et al. (2019), the power analysis was specified with an effect size of d = 0.063, a residual variance of 0.61, a participant intercept variance of 0.23, an item intercept variance of 0.16, and participant-by-item, participant-slope, and item-slope variances set to 0. PANGEA power calculations indicated that a sample size of 30 participants per experiment (i.e., spaced x unspaced in young adults (Experiments 1 and 2) and spaced x unspaced in older adults (Experiments 3 and 4) reading 209 items would yield statistical power exceeding 1 -ẞ = .80 for the target two-way interaction effects.

To achieve this, we recruited 60 younger adults (30 assigned to unspaced and 30 assigned to spaced conditions) and 30 older adults (who completed both spaced and unspaced conditions). Whereas previous eye-tracking benchmarks in compound reading relied on smaller item sets (e.g., 120 items in Juhasz, 2018), testing all 209 items led to 90 participants producing a total of 25,080 trials, maximising statistical power by substantially reducing item-level standard errors (Brysbaert, 2018).

Crucially, rather than relying solely on pre-experimental frequentist power thresholds, our primary statistical inference was conducted within a Bayesian mixed-effects framework (Gelman et al., 2014). Bayesian estimation evaluates the posterior probability distribution given the exact observed data rather than long-run Type II error rates under hypothetical parameters.

Participants

A final sample of 90 participants took part in the study. Thirty young adults (18-24 years) participated in Experiment 1; a second group of 30 young adults (18-23 years) participated in Experiment 2; and 30 older adults (61-85 years) participated in Experiments 3 and 4. A further three young adults were excluded from Experiment 1 due to experimenter error in recording eye-movement data, and one further young adult was excluded from Experiment 2 for reporting dyslexia. The young adult participants were first-and second-year undergraduate students from the School of Psychology and Vision Sciences at the University of Leicester. Older adult participants were recruited from the local community in Leicester. In accordance with APA guidelines, we reported the self-declared ethnic heritage of the participants, confirming the diversity of the UK sample. Importantly, all participants were classed as native British English speakers: all participants completed their education within the British education system and reported using British English as their primary language from the age of three years. The study received ethical approval from the University of Leicester Ethics Committee (ref: 39830). All participants provided written informed consent prior to participation. Young adults received course credit in exchange for participation, while older adults were compensated with a £30 voucher per experiment (£60 total). All participants reported normal or corrected-to-normal vision and identified English as their primary language. Table 1 provides a summary of participant characteristics. In accordance with best practices for handling missing data (Woods et al., 2023), the missing data rate for all demographic and individual difference data in the samples was low (less than 1%) and confirmed to be Missing at Random across experiments. The two age groups were matched for years of formal education (see Table 2). The older adults were screened for cognitive impairment using the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA), with a standard exclusion criterion of scores below 26 out of 30 (Nasreddine et al., 2005).

Participants' visual capabilities were confirmed using three standard assessments: the Bailey-Lovie (Bailey & Lovie, 1976), the Early Treatment Diabetic Retinopathy Study (ETDRS) chart (Ferris & Bailey, 1996), and the Pelli-Robson tests (Pelli, Robson & Wilkins, 1988). These assessments verified that all participants had been properly corrected for the specific viewing distance of the experimental screen. As is typical, older adults showed lower visual acuity than young adults. Older adults also showed lower sensitivity to higher spatial frequencies than young adults (log contrast sensitivity: Experiment 1: M = 1.89 (young adults); Experiment 2: M = 2.08 (young adults), M = 1.54 (older adults), again typical for these age groups (e.g., see Owsley, 2016).

We used independent t tests to assess whether there were significant between-group differences in the individual difference measures (see Table 2). Additional assessments included the Vocabulary subtest from the WAIS-III and the WAIS-III Digit Span subtest (Wechsler, 1997). There were no significant differences in digit span between young adults and the older adults. Print exposure and vocabulary knowledge was lower in young adults relative to older adults, as is typical (Salthouse, 2019). Despite the young adults in Experiment 2 also performed significantly better on the Title Recognition Test than the young adults in Experiment 1, this did not survive Holm-Bonferroni correction. (Elsherif et al., 2021 (Elsherif et al., , 2022 (Elsherif et al., , 2023 (Elsherif et al., , 2025 (Elsherif et al., , 2026)). Note that vocabulary and digit span scores reflect task-specific performance rather than absolute measures of vocabulary or memory capacity. We used Holm-Bonferroni to control for multiple comparisons.

Materials

We used the 211 unspaced compound words and sentences from Juhasz (2018). The compound words were primarily noun-noun compounds (see Supplementary Materials). The sentences were adapted to ensure suitability for native British English speakers. Word length values were obtained from Juhasz et al.'s (2015) database, and word frequencies (in Zipf values) were extracted from the SUBTLEX-UK database for the full compound, as well as for the modifier and head lexemes (van Heuven et al., 2014). In addition, each target word was coded dichotomously (1 = presence, -1 = absence) for the following phonetic features: bilabial, labiodental, dental, labiovelar, postalveolar, alveolar, palatal, palatal-alveolar, glottal, velar, and voiced. Although such coding is typically used in naming studies to control for initial phoneme effects, we applied it here to ensure that eye-tracking results were not confounded by uncontrolled phonetic complexity. These phonetic details are reported in the Supplementary Materials. Stimulus characteristics from Juhasz (2018) are presented in Table 3, and example sentences are shown in Table 4. We used independent t tests to assess whether there were significant between-group differences in the individual difference measures.The average sentence length was 12.61 (SD = 1.50). The same sentences were used for unspaced compound words and spaced compound words. To create spaced compound words, a space was inserted between the modifier and head constituents. (van Heuven et al., 2014). Ratings for familiarity, imageability, AoA, Semantic Transparency, and Lexeme Meaning Dominance were collected using 7-or 10-point Likert scales, as indicated. The compound words had previously been normed for a North American population (see Juhasz et al., 2015). We therefore collected new normative data online, using Prolific, to ensure that the stimuli were appropriate for a UK population. The new normative data were obtained from another 32 young adults, aged 18-36, and 32 older adults, aged 60-83 years, who did not take part in the eye-movement experiments. We used the norming tasks and instructions from Juhasz et al. (2015) to obtain ratings (on a 1-7 Likert scale) for the AoA, imageability, and familiarity of each compound word, and its component lexemes. We also collected ratings for semantic transparency (the extent to which the meanings of the constituents relate to the meaning of the compound word, e.g., "door" in "doorbell") on a 7point Likert scale. Additionally, we collected ratings for lexeme meaning dominance (the degree to which the meaning of the compound is captured by its modifier and head lexemes) on a 10-point Likert scale. Furthermore, we obtained scores for naturalness ratings, using a 7-point Likert scale from 1 (completely unnatural) to 7 (natural), in which participants rated the naturalness of the sentence. In addition, we conducted a cloze task to assess participants' ability to predict the target word in the sentence. On each trial, participants were presented with a partial sentence and asked to provide the expected compound word. The score for each target word was the proportion of participants that correctly generated the given word. After the cloze task, participants viewed the sentence together with the correct target word and were asked to rate the naturalness of the complete sentence. We additionally asked 20 native British English speakers to rate their preference for the spaced and unspaced versions of each compound word in British English, on a 7-point Likert scale.

Ratings for all measures were averaged across participants and age groups. Table 3 provides a summary of the average normative ratings. Additional details, including task instructions, are available in the Supplementary Materials.

Apparatus and procedure

Young adults participated in a single session lasting approximately 2 hoursfoot_0 , completing both the individual difference measures (see Table 2) and the eye-tracking tasks. Thirty young adults read unspaced compound words in sentences (Experiment 1), while another thirty young adults read spaced compound words in sentences (Experiment 2). Older adults completed two separate eye-tracking sessions: one for the unspaced and one for the spaced compound words. Due to the practical challenges of recruiting from the older adult population, a within-subjects design was employed for the spacing manipulation to maximize statistical power and account for individual variability. To control for potential order effects and practice effects associated with the within-subjects design, the order of the spacing manipulation was fully counterbalanced across older adult participants. Participants were randomly assigned to one of two conditions: those who completed the unspaced session first and those who completed the spaced session first. Each older adult session consisted of instructions, task completion and post-task assessments, with Session 1 lasting approximately two hours and Session 2 lasting one hour. The sessions were split by seven days, to minimise potential carryover, learning, and fatigue effects. Therefore, the total duration for each older adult participant across the entire study was approximately 3 hours.

Participants were tested individually in a dimmed room. Eye movements were recorded via an Eyelink 1000 Plus tower-mounted eye-tracker (SR Research, Ltd., Canada).

This system has an angular resolution of less than .01 Root Mean Square. Right-eye movements were sampled at 1000Hz using corneal reflection and pupil tracking. A chin and forehead rest were used to reduce head movements, and a VPixx response box was used to collect manual responses. Sentences were displayed on a 19-inch monitor, at a 60 cm viewing distance, with each letter subtended approximately 1° horizontally. Sentence stimuli were displayed in 14-point Courier New font as black text on a white background. Sentences were shown as a single line of text.

Participants were instructed to read each sentence naturally and for comprehension.

At the start of the experiment, a 3-point horizontal calibration was performed along the same line as the sentence presentation, ensuring spatial accuracy of 0.30° or better for all participants. Calibration accuracy was checked before each trial. To maintain high spatial precision throughout the session, recalibration was conducted whenever a participant took a break and additionally at the experimenter's discretion. At the start of each trial, a fixation cross (equal in size to one character space) appeared on the left side of the display. Once the participant fixated this location, the cross disappeared, and the sentence stimulus was presented, with its first letter replacing the cross. Participants were instructed to read each sentence naturally and silently, and to then look toward a fixation point located to the right of the sentence. They were also instructed to press a key on a response box to indicate that they had completed reading. The sentence then disappeared and was either followed by a comprehension question or the next trial.

Comprehension questions were presented on 24% of trials. Half the questions required a "yes" response and half a "no" response. Participants responded by pressing one of two keys on the response box. For unspaced compound words, response accuracy was 96% and 97% for young and older adults, respectively; for spaced compound words, accuracy was 98% for both groups. Participants were offered breaks approximately every 15 minutes and could take additional breaks as needed.

Data Cleaning

Once data collection was complete, we used SR Research DataViewer to process and prepare the eye-tracking data for analysis. We then pre-processed the data following standard quality-control protocols for reading eye-tracking paradigms (e.g., Inhoff & Radach, 1998; Rayner, 1998). First, we removed long fixations exceeding 1200ms, as indicators of tracking artefacts or tracker loss. Following that step, we combined brief fixations to account for oculomotor drift and small saccadic corrections. Fixations lasting less than 80ms that occurred within 0.5 of the visual angle of an adjacent fixation were combined, as were fixations under 120 ms occurring within 1.25 degrees apart (see review by Drieghe et al., 2026). Any remaining unmerged fixations with durations under 80ms were discarded, as they fall below the perceptual threshold necessary for lexical processing. Data loss constituted 0.77% of the total data. We then also removed the compound word 'background', as participants scored more than 80% error on the associated comprehension question; this represented a data loss of 0.48% of the remaining data. Bayesian models were implemented using the "brms" package (version 2.15.0; Bürkner, 2020). Data and analysis code for all experiments are available at https://osf.io/b5zja. Here, we report how we determined our sample size, exclusions, all manipulations, and measures in the study. All analyses, including outlier rejection, handling of missing data, and inferential criteria, were pre-registered on the Open Science Framework (https://osf.io/cqf7g). The total sample size and exclusion criteria were determined prior to data collection.

Analysis procedure

To investigate whether the AoA effect on compound word processing is modulated by age and orthographic spacing, our analysis proceeds in two stages. First, we provide granular Bayesian sub-analyses for each experimental condition (spaced and unspaced, for both young and older adults). Second, we integrate the data from all conditions into a global linear mixed-effects model (the primary analysis). This approach directly tests the three-way interaction between age, spacing, and our core lexical predictors to evaluate the Integrated Account. This multi-stage approach ensures that our conclusions regarding the high-level interaction are anchored by the established, robust presence of AoA effects at the individual condition level.

We used a hybrid statistical approach to ensure the robustness of our findings. The Bayesian sub-analyses provide a nuanced estimation of individual effects without the binary constraints of traditional significance testing, allowing for a granular examination of AoA across conditions. Conversely, our global analysis uses Likelihood Ratio Tests to demonstrate that the three-way interaction provides a significantly better fit to the data than simpler models. By verifying our results across both statistical philosophies, we establish that our findings are not artifacts of a single methodological framework. Details of these models are provided below, beginning with our sub-analyses.

We started with four models, to assess the effect of psycholinguistic predictors on the processing of spaced and unspaced compound words in young and older adults separately.

Models 1 and 2 examined unspaced and spaced compound words in young adults respectively. Models 3 and 4 examined unspaced and spaced compound words in older adults respectively. In the baseline models, the mean-centred fixed effects were: compound word frequency, frequency of both the modifier and head lexemes, and word length of the compound word (see supplementary materials for baseline models). The outcome variables were the following standard eye-movement measures on the target compound word (see Rayner, 2009): FFD, SFD, GD and total reading time. FFD, SFD and GD are measures sensitive to initial (i.e., first-pass) processing of the target word, prior to a fixation to its right or a regression to its left, whereas total reading time is a measure for later processing of reading. Duration measures were log-transformed to address issues of skewness and normality of distribution (Wang et al., 2019). For the influence of these predictors on raw duration measures using frequentist statistics, and for additional robustness checks, see supplementary materials 3 . Additional mean-centred predictors of interest (compound word familiarity, AoA, imageability, semantic transparency, and lexeme meaning dominance) were entered individually into the baseline models, for each duration measure (see Juhasz et al., 2015; Juhasz, 2018; Kuperman, 2013) (see Figure 1 for correlations between the variables).

All models used a maximal random effects structure; if they did not converge (Veldre & Andrews, 2015), the random structures for both participants and items were reduced until convergence was attained, down to random intercepts. For all Bayesian models, we used weakly informative/regularising priors (Lemoine, 2019; McElreath, 2020) on the random slope coefficients: Normal(0, 1). Our models used weakly informative priors of Normal(0, 1) for each fixed effect. Other than changing the prior of the slope coefficient, we used the default priors chosen by brms. These priors would be considered weakly informative and produce minimal influence on model predictions. Models were run initially with four chains of 4,000 iterations each (2,000 iterations discarded after warmup). Additional iterations were added in cases where the output of a model suggested a convergence issue. For models with a continuous outcome variable, the model family was set to lognormal. MCMC sampling was satisfactory (no divergent transitions, all Rhat values = 1.0). For each statistical model, we report the median effect estimate (the most probable effect size) alongside a 95% credible interval (the range of values containing the parameter with 95% probability) and p(>0) or p(<0) (the probability that the variable's effect is positive or negative, respectively). We interpret a variable as having evidence for an effect if its 95% credible interval does not include zero and the directional probability, p(>0) or p(<0), is 0.99 or higher (Kruschke et al., 2012; Nicenboim & Vasishth, 2016), as this minimises the likelihood of the effect being in the opposite direction. It is important to note that this directional probability indicates the certainty of the effect's sign, assuming an effect is present, rather than the probability that the effect exists in the first place. Posterior predictive checks showed that the models we used could reasonably have generated the data.

All primary Bayesian models were parameterised with crossed random intercepts for participants and items. Continuous item-level covariates were excluded from the primary models due to substantial computational load and prolonged MCMC sampling durations across our 25080 observations. To confirm that excluding participant-level AoA random slopes did not artificially inflate directional certainty or bias fixed-effect estimates, sensitivity analyses were conducted on subset models specifying random slopes for AoA (1+AoA|participant), demonstrating that the conclusions are robust to random slope parameterisation.

Following the granular sub-analyses, we integrated data from both age groups and spacing conditions to formally test the Integrated Account of AoA. As established in our introduction, this account posits that lexical retrieval is a dynamic process where cognitive demands, such as those imposed by non-canonical spacing or age-related changes, are modulated by a word's AoA. If this framework holds, we should observe that the processing of compound words is not merely the sum of independent factors, but a complex interaction where AoA acts as a buffer against the processing costs associated with spacing and ageing.

To specifically test whether AoA and familiarity and Imageability can be disentangled, we compared models containing both terms, Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC). Note that for effects where the likelihood ratio test yielded a critical value near the standard statistical significance threshold (X2 = 3.84 to 4.50), BIC values show a slight increase. This reflects the conservative complexity penalty function of BIC under large sample sizes (N), where a model's log-likelihood fit improvement (X2) must exceed the penalty term ln(N) to achieve a decrease in BIC. We report both metrics for transparency, relying on likelihood ratio tests for hypothesis testing.

To evaluate this, we conducted a global linear mixed-effects model assessing the three-way interaction of age, spacing, and our core lexical predictors (frequency, familiarity, AoA, and imageability). This model serves as the primary analysis to answer our core research question: whether older readers can overcome the structural costs of spaced compound words through the established advantages of early-acquired lexical representations. Fixed effects were sum-coded to allow for a direct assessment of group and condition differences (spacing: -1 = unspaced,1 = spaced; age: -1 = older adults,1 = young adults).

Results

Results across the lifespan?

RQ1: Is the AoA effect present in orthographic spacing

Descriptive statistics for all eye-tracking measures across age groups and spacing conditions are summarised in Table 5. Mean fixation durations across measures (FFD, SFD, GD, and TFD) were systematically longer for spaced, relative to unspaced, compound words across both age groupsfoot_2 . Older adults generally showed longer late-stage reading measures (GD and TFD) compared to younger adults, particularly in the spaced compound condition.

Bayesian analyses.

Across both age groups and spacing conditions (Tables 5 6 7), AoA and familiarity emerged as robust predictors of lexical retrieval in most conditions. Specifically, AoA remained a consistent influence for young adults across both spaced and unspaced conditions, and for older adults reading unspaced compound words (P > .99). In these models, we observed a reliable AoA effect, where earlier-acquired words were associated with shorter fixation durations. The same pattern held for familiarity, where higher familiarity consistently predicted reduced fixation durations (P > .99). Imageability showed a more selective influence, primarily impacting SFD and GD for unspaced compound words and GD and TFD for spaced compound words, such that the more imageable the compound word, the smaller fixation duration.

To evaluate whether whole-compound AoA accounts for incremental variance during the eye-tracking of unspaced and spaced compound words, beyond collinear subjective frequency control variables such as familiarity and semantic variables such as imageability, we conducted stepwise likelihood ratio tests holding baseline variables constant. In contrast, a qualitative shift in processing strategy was evident in older adults reading spaced compound words. In this condition, neither AoA nor imageability remained significant predictors of reading times. Instead, processing became time-locked to constituent-level metrics: Semantic Transparency predicted SFD, TFD, whereas LMD influenced SFD and familiarity emerged as a predictor for TFD only. The more semantically transparent, rightheaded and familiar the compound, the smaller the fixation duration, indicating faster retrieval. These findings suggest that for older adults, the structural disruption introduced by a space forces a move away from global word-level processing toward a fragmented, lexeme-dependent strategy (see Tables S6-S17 for full baseline and exploratory models).

RQ2: How do orthographic spacing and age interact to influence the AoA effect during compound word processing?

To formally test the Integrated Account, we integrated data across all groups into a global model to assess the predicted two-way interaction between age and AoA and spacing and AoA (Table 10; See Table S17 for three-way interaction). We observed that spacing affected all duration measures (SFD: b = 0.028, SE = 0.010, CrI

Spacing * Psycholinguistic Variables

We examined the influence of lexical-semantic properties, including frequency, imageability, familiarity and AoA during silent reading in spaced and unspaced compound word. Crucially, we observed reliable two-way interactions between orthographic spacing and whole-word psycholinguistic properties (Table 10). While earlier-acquired, higher-frequency, highly familiar, and highly imageable compound words consistently yielded shorter reading times overall, the facilitative slopes for AoA, word frequency, familiarity, and imageability were significantly steeper for unspaced compound words than for spaced compound words. This indicates that visual separation attenuates the immediate processing advantage conferred by whole-word lexical-semantic properties.

Ageing * Psycholinguistic Variables

We examined the influence of lexical-semantic properties, including frequency, imageability, familiarity and AoA during silent reading across younger and older adults. The global model revealed a significant two-way interaction between reader age and whole-word AoA and familiarity (Table 10). Specifically, the facilitative slopes for both AoA and familiarity were significantly steeper in younger adults than in older adults. While younger adults showed a marked reduction in fixation durations for early-acquired and highly familiar compounds, this processing advantage was flatter in older adults, consistent with the hypothesis that cumulative lifelong reading exposure narrows the processing efficiency gap between earlyand late-acquired words 9.

General Discussion

The present study used eye-tracking to investigate how AoA influences compound word processing, focusing specifically on how these effects are modulated by younger and older adults and word spacing. Our findings revealed that the age at which participants learned a compound word significantly influenced eye movements during reading. Words acquired earlier in life were generally associated with fewer fixations in young adults, across spaced and unspaced compound words. This supports previous findings, that the AoA of compound words, whether presented spaced or unspaced, influences eye movements in young adults (Juhasz, 2018). However, in older adults, we only observed an AoA effect during the reading of unspaced compound words.

RQ1: AoA, orthographic spacing across the lifespan Lexical Access in Young Adults: The Impact of AoA and Spacing

When reading unspaced and spaced compound words, we observed in young adults that the AoA of the compound (as well as its familiarity) contributed to processing across eyetracking measures, replicating Juhasz (2018). Here, we observed that there were fewer and smaller fixations on words that were acquired earlier, as well as on words that were more frequent and more familiar. This indicates that unspaced and spaced compound words are processed more quickly when they are acquired earlier in life, in eye-movement measures that reflect both early first-pass reading and later syntactic integration. The observation of an AoA effect in both unspaced and spaced compound words further indicates that these words are processed as a single lexical representation, rather than as individual constituents, irrespective of spacing. An effect of word length was also observed, but only in gaze duration and total fixation duration for unspaced compound words, and in all measures except total fixation duration for spaced compound words.

There was an interaction between AoA and spacing in young adults. Across first fixation duration, single fixation duration and gaze duration, the slope of the AoA effect was steeper when the compound word was presented as an unspaced item, rather than as a spaced item. Thus, we observed that the AoA effect was stronger when processing requires direct access to the whole-word lexical representation, rather than via the constituent morphemes. In spaced compound words, the spacing splits the compound word into its two constituents. This potentially introduces initial competition between the meaning of the compound word and the meanings of its constituent morphemes, at first diluting the facilitatory effect of acquiring the compound word earlier in life. However, in total fixation duration, the slope of the AoA effect was steeper when the compound word was presented as a spaced item, rather than as an unspaced item. Thus, in total fixation duration, which indexes processing time once readers have integrated the constituent morphemes into a single lexical representation, there is no longer any competition-mediated dilution of the AoA effect. Instead, the AoA effect is strengthened, with readers benefitting from having acquired both the constituents, and the whole compound, earlier in life (Brooks & de Garcia, 2015).

This process is also reflected in imageability, which was stronger for spaced compound words than unspaced compound words in total fixation duration, indicating that the AoA has a lexical-semantic component.

Lexical Access in Older Adults: The Influence of Linguistic Entrenchment

When reading unspaced compound words, we observed in older adults that the AoA of the compound (as well as its familiarity) contributed to processing across eye-tracking measures. Here, we observed that there were fewer and smaller fixations on words that were acquired earlier, as well as on words that were more frequent and more familiar. This indicates that unspaced compound words are processed more quickly when they are acquired earlier in life, in eye-movement measures that reflect both early first-pass reading and later syntactic integration. The observation of an AoA effect in unspaced compound words indicates that these words were being processed as a single lexical representation, rather than as individual constituents. The findings also support the suggestion that the AoA effect can be observed from the point of early first-pass measures, which index low-level processing between orthography and phonology, in line with Elsherif and Catling's (2021, 2023) argument.

Critically, these results underscore the role of linguistic entrenchment in the mature lexicon.

Despite decades of additional language experience, older adults demonstrate that the lexical-semantic networks formed early in life remain highly stable and efficient (e.g., Davies et al., 2017). This entrenchment allows older readers to maintain a unified processing strategy for unspaced compounds, effectively leveraging their long-standing linguistic knowledge to facilitate rapid whole-word retrieval. By maintaining this consistent AoA advantage, older adults demonstrate that their mental lexicon does not merely expand or degrade with age, but rather becomes more refined, allowing for the stable, efficient processing of familiar, early-acquired word forms when they are presented in their standard orthographic configuration. An effect of word length was also observed in unspaced compound words, but only in gaze duration and total fixation duration, indicating lengthbased processing remains a secondary, later-stage constraint compared to the primary influence of AoA and familiarity.

In older adults, the processing of spaced compound words was unaffected by AoA across all eye-tracking measures. We observed effects of only word length and semantic transparency in gaze duration and total fixation duration. Thus, shorter compound words received shorter fixations than longer compound words and semantically transparent compound words received fewer fixations than semantically opaque compound words. An effect of familiarity was only observed in total fixation duration. In older adults, the absence of an AoA effect in spaced compound words likely stems from the dual nature of linguistic entrenchment in the mature lexicon (Ramscar et al., 2014). Through decades of cumulative language exposure, older adults develop highly entrenched, rigid orthographic-semantic representations for unspaced compounds. Consequently, encountering an artificially spaced compound (e.g., sweet corn) severely violates these entrenched orthographic expectations, causing an immediate parsing failure that is further exacerbated by age-related reductions in perceptual span (Rayner et al., 2006; Zhang et al., 2023). Because this unexpected space is included, it impedes direct lexical access and forces older adults to rely on lower-level, early word-level attributes like length (Inhoff et al., 2000). This effectively allows AoA to be bypassed by immediate low-level processing. Furthermore, because artificially spaced compounds are initially misparsed as orthographically illegal non-compounds, the reading process becomes bottlenecked at the low-level orthographic stages. During this stage, lexical-semantic variables (e.g. ,AoA) are prevented from producing their influence on gaze duration and total fixation durations, thereby constraining the extent to which relational semantic properties (e.g., semantic transparency) can facilitate reading times. Crucially these constraints persist despite semantic processing typically playing a larger role in longer words (Cortese & Schock, 2013).

Importantly, this orthographic expectation manifests primarily in early eye-movement metrics: age-related divergence between young and older adults was shown in FFD and SFD, capturing the initial perceptual parsing and constituent processing of first lexeme. In contrast, in TFD, which indexes late stage semantic integration and re-reading, AoA and spacing became highly similar between young and older adults. This indicates while orthographic familiarity, entrenched expectations, and reduced visual span disrupts early constituent recognition for older adults temporarily, while late-stage lexical integration and semantic consolidation operate similarly across age groups once the full compound structure is evaluated.

We can therefore conclude that the processing of compound words relies on a shifting balance between orthographic cues and long-term lexical knowledge, which evolves significantly across the lifespan.

RQ2: The Interaction of Orthographic Spacing or Age on Compound Processing

Furthermore, we investigated the interactions between spacing and AoA. We found that unspaced compound words showed the largest effects of AoA. In total fixation duration, the AoA effect was stronger in spaced than unspaced compound words. The divergence between early and late measures suggests that while AoA initially facilitates the holistic recognition of unspaced compounds, its role shifts during the later stages of processing for spaced compounds. The presence of a space forces the reader to work harder to assemble the meaning of the two parts. This creates a larger processing gap: early-acquired words remain easy to synthesize because the brain has strong, pre-existing 'shortcuts' for them, whereas later-acquired words require significantly more effort to combine, leading to longer fixation durations. This aligns with the representation theory proposed by Brysbaert et al. (2000), which posits that the semantic nodes for early-acquired words are more centrally located and more densely connected with the mental lexicon. Consequently, these findings suggest that the AoA is a structural characteristic of how linguistic information is organised and retrieved across the lifespan. This process is also reflected in imageability, familiarity, and frequency which was stronger for spaced compound words than unspaced compound words in total fixation duration, indicating that the AoA has a lexical-semantic component.

We also observed a two-way interaction between ageing and AoA. The influence of AoA was less pronounced in older adults compared to younger adults, as observed across all duration measures. The reduced AoA effect in older readers may reflect a shift in how the mental lexicon organises itself over time. Specifically, as the semantic network becomes more dense with age, the foundational nodes established by early-acquired words provide a more efficient framework for processing complex compounds, leading to a decline in the AoA effect. This process is also reflected in imageability, familiarity, and frequency which showed an age-related decline such that these measures decrease with age. Additionally, the finding that the AoA effect is partially aligned with the suggestion the AoA effect is a result of time: early-acquired words are processed more quickly only because, having been learned first, they are encountered significantly more often over the course of the lifespan than words acquired later (i.e., the cumulative frequency explanation; Lewis, 1999).

On the other hand, in line with Monaghan and Ellis (2010), the finding that the AoA effect lessens with age may reflect a shift in network efficiency: as the semantic system matures and becomes more interconnected, the structural headstart provided by early-acquired nodes may become less vital for fluent compound word processing.

The interaction of spacing and AoA, as well as the interaction between AoA and ageing can be both explained by the integrated account. According to this framework, the In contrast, the age-related decline of the AoA effect reflects the developmental changes within the semantic hub itself. Over decades of cumulative reading experience, later-acquired words received repeated exposures and continued semantic integration (see Bybee, 2011 for further explanation). This lifelong exposure solidifies late-learned representations within the semantic network, effectively narrowing the structural processing gap between early-and late-acquired compound words. In older adults, the semantic hub becomes highly dense and interconnected. Consequently, the advantage of early-acquired words over late-acquired words becomes less critical for fluent holistic word recognition. Our results reveal that the AoA effect depends on the direct mapping and maturational state of the semantic network, which is in line with linguistic entrenchment for older adults (Davies et al., 2017).

While our primary focus rests on the two-way interactions (Spacing * AoA, Age * AoA), evaluating the full interaction pattern helps illustrate the operational limits of lexical processing across conditions. Unspaced compounds maintain a consistent, albeit smaller, AoA advantage across the adult lifespan. In contrast, spaced compounds exhibit a floor effect in older adults, where the structural disruption of the space combined with age-related orthographic rigidity eliminates the whole-word AoA advantage. In line with the Integrated Account (Brysbaert & Ellis, 2016; Chang et al., 2019; Elsherif et al., 2023), these pattern differences demonstrate that whole-word AoA influences processing primarily when readers can access holistic representations, whereas visual disruption forces older readers to shift toward constituent-level parsing (for full three-way model parameters and extended theoretical breakdown, see Supplementary Material Table S17).

Implications for Models of Eye Movement Control

The findings from this study could also inform the development of quantitative models of eye movement control, particularly those designed for monolingual, native language reading.

Examples of existing models include E-Z Reader (e.g., Rayner et al., 2006; Reichle, 2021; Reichle et al., 2012) and SWIFT (e.g., Engbert et al., 2005; Laubrock et al., 2006). For instance, E-Z Reader has successfully simulated how eye movements in reading differ with age (Rayner et al., 2006; Laubrock et al., 2006 showed similar results with SWIFT). While E-Z Reader primarily focuses on the word frequency effect, it can, in theory, explain AoArelated reading development in children by considering cumulative frequency. More specifically, E-Z Reader suggests that the initial stages of accessing a word are influenced by its properties, including how often it occurs. Words learned later in life are generally encountered less often and have lower subjective frequencies than words learned earlier.

However, it is important to clarify that this is not a universal rule for all words acquired throughout life. Some words learned later might be encountered more frequently and have higher subjective frequencies but still be processed more slowly than earlier-acquired words.

Crucially, the current version of the E-Z Reader model addresses AoA only indirectly. While cumulative frequency and a word's frequency trajectory during development do correlate with AoA, the model lacks explicit mechanisms to capture the subtle, potentially qualitative differences in how words are represented and processed due to AoA itself (Zevin & Seidenberg, 2002 , 2004). For example, AoA effects often remain even when frequency is accounted for, indicating that the timing of learning uniquely impacts how words are stored and accessed. Therefore, future adaptations of models such as E-Z Reader, especially when considering the entire lifespan, would benefit from including direct parameters that account for AoA's independent contributions to how we process words and control our eye movements during reading.

Limitations

Although our preliminary analyses incorporated phonological controls to manage noise in reading data, we have chosen to use more parsimonious models for this report. This approach was adopted to secure more stable regression estimates and mitigate the risks associated with overparameterisation (Achen, 2005). By transitioning to more parsimonious models, we secured more reliable estimates and mitigated the risk of Type I errors associated with high-dimensional model structures. Crucially, our subsequent Bayesian analysis demonstrated that the core AoA effects remained robust regardless of this simplification. This process therefore served as a rigorous validation step, significantly increasing our confidence in the consistency and stability of these findings.

A further limitation of our stimuli relates to the representation of spaced compound words.

While we included unspaced compounds, our set did not feature compounds that are conventionally spaced in natural language (e.g., 'fast food'). Consequently, our findings may not fully capture the processing nuances involved in reading natural, open-compound forms, which differ structurally from both closed-form compounds and simple non-compound words.

Future research should prioritise the inclusion of these naturally spaced compounds to determine if the morphological decomposition processes we observed remain consistent when the orthographic boundary is explicitly marked by a space, rather than implied through constituent combination to enhance the study's ecological validity.

We must also note a limitation in our experimental design regarding participant allocation.

While our younger adult cohort consisted of two distinct groups, 30 participants for the unspaced condition and a separate 30 for the spaced condition, our older adult sample comprised 30 individuals who completed both conditions. To mitigate potential confounding variables such as practice effects or cumulative fatigue inherent in within-subjects designs, we implemented a mandatory one-week interval between testing sessions to minimise carryover effects and the order of the spaced and unspaced conditions was systematically counterbalanced across participants for older adults. While these measures were designed to isolate the effects of the experimental conditions, future research should aim for a fully independent design across all cohorts to further ensure that performance is not inadvertently influenced by variations in exposure or testing order.

Conclusion

In conclusion, our research provides robust evidence for the influence of AoA on compound word processing, though the manifestation of this effect is modulated by both format and cognitive task. Our eye-tracking data suggests that while AoA influences all levels of lexical retrieval in young adults, this effect is attenuated in older adults, likely due to increased semantic entrenchment. Our findings also reveal a critical boundary: the effect is modulated by compound format in older adults. This suggests that the mental lexicon undergoes a qualitative shift with age. The space in compound words forces a transition toward constituent-level processing; because spaced constituents are orthographically distinct, they likely compete for lexical selection rather than converging into a unified representation.

Consequently, the structural integration typically afforded to early-acquired words is disrupted. We propose that because the ageing lexicon is more densely interconnected, older adults rely on a highly entrenched, unified semantic structure. When a compound word is presented with a space, this structure is challenged; the reader must resolve the competition between the individual lexemes and the compound entry itself, a process that negates the processing advantage of early acquisition. This refinement to the Integrated Account highlights that while AoA remains a fundamental driver of lexical retrieval, its manifestation is sensitive to the interplay between linguistic format and the adaptive plasticity of the ageing brain. While existing eye-tracking models can partially account for our findings, it remains an open question as to whether quantitative models of eye-movement control, developed primarily to explain word frequency (such as E-Z Reader and SWIFT), can formally simulate the observed AoA effect across the lifespan in more complex words.

Addressing this gap will be crucial for developing a truly unified theory of reading that accounts for how lexical plasticity and orthographic complexity interact as we age.

We deviated from our pre-registration by examining two-way interactions (AoA * aging and AoA * spacing) rather than three-way interactions (AoA * aging * spacing). This adjustment was made because our sample lacked sufficient statistical power to test three-way interactions. To adhere to principles of Open Scholarship, analysis and figures for the three-way interactions are provided in the Supplementary Materials.

AoA advantage arises from entrenched orthographic-to-phonological mappings formed during early developmental periods of heightened neuroplasticity (Mapping Theory) and the central positioning of early acquired words within the densely connected semantic hub (Representation Account). The decline of the AoA effect from spaced to unspaced compound words, alongside its age-related decline, indicates that these interactions reflect different mechanisms within the integrated account. Introducing a space into conventional compound words disrupts the immediate, direct mapping between orthographic representation and the whole-word compound word semantic entry. This visual separation forces the cognitive system into constituent-level decomposition, triggering competition between the constituent lexemes and the full compound entry. During early first-pass reading (FFD, SFD, GD), this constituent competition dilutes the immediate processing advantage conferred by early whole-word acquisition. Visual disruption, therefore, temporarily masks the mapping component during initial lexical access, shifting early processing reliance onto constituent-level properties.
